questions.prompt: In the toy predictor trained on "the cat sat . the cat ran . the dog sat .", what probability does it give to "dog" coming after "the"?
options: About 0.67, because "dog" is one of two animals
About 0.33, because "the" is followed by "dog" 1 time out of 3
0.5, because there are two possible next words
1, because "dog" always follows "the" when it appears
questions.explanation: "the" appears 3 times: twice before "cat" and once before "dog". So "dog" gets 1 out of 3, about 0.33, and the probabilities 0.67 and 0.33 add up to 1.

questions.prompt: You ask a model the same question twice and get two slightly different replies. Why?
options: The model looked the answer up in two different places
The model changed its learned numbers after the first question
The model often draws its next piece at random, weighted by the probabilities
The first reply was cut short by the keyboard
questions.explanation: A model does not always take the most likely option. It often picks at random in proportion to the probabilities, so two runs can choose different pieces and drift apart.

questions.prompt: A model confidently states a wrong date for a historical event. What best explains this?
options: It predicts likely text rather than checking facts, so a likely-sounding wrong answer comes out fluently
It found a wrong source while searching the web
It ran out of probability for the correct answer
It only looks at the last word of the question
questions.explanation: A model writes whatever continuation it scores as likely. It never looks facts up, so when the likely-sounding continuation is wrong it is written in the same confident tone.
